title: OpenAI retiring GPT-4o in Jan 2027
content:
GPT-6 Luna is the recommended starting point for migrating existing GPT-4.x use cases. The right configuration depends on your application, so evaluate the model on representative workloads before moving production traffic.
Choose your reasoning setting
Start with reasoning effort set to none. Most GPT-4.x use cases are expected to migrate with this setting. Test other settings to find the right balance of quality, latency, and cost for your application.
For API changes and technical details, see the GPT-6 developer guide.
Compare cost and performance
GPT-6 Luna has a lower per-token price than the GPT-4.x models covered by this migration. For most use cases, it offers a more capable model at a lower per-token price.
Compare total cost on your own workloads before migrating. Token usage and reasoning settings can affect the cost of each task.
Migrate your application
- Establish a baseline. Select representative requests, including important edge cases, and record your current model’s quality, latency, and cost.
- Evaluate Luna. Start with reasoning effort set to none and compare results against your baseline. Check the behaviors your application depends on, including output formatting and tool use where relevant.
- Tune and retest. Adjust prompts, reasoning effort, and verbosity based on your evaluation results, then retest.
- Roll out gradually. Begin with a limited share of production traffic. Monitor quality, latency, errors, and cost before completing the migration.
Get support
Self-serve customers: Contact OpenAI Support through the chat bubble at help.openai.com.
Sales-managed customers: Contact your OpenAI account team to arrange support from our engineering team. We can help develop a migration plan tailored to your product and identify how to get the most out of Luna.

report.summary: OpenAI will retire GPT-4o and other GPT-4.x models in January 2027, directing developers to migrate production workloads to the cheaper, more capable GPT-6 Luna.
report.background: GPT-4o arrived in May 2024 as OpenAI's flagship multimodal model and quickly became the default backbone for chatbots, agents, RAG pipelines, and copilots across the industry. Since then, the frontier has shifted toward reasoning models that spend extra compute at inference time, and toward consolidating sprawling model lineups into fewer, cheaper families. Meanwhile, aggressive open-weight competition has pushed per-token prices down sharply, making older flagship models expensive relative to their capability. Deprecation notices are now a routine part of the commercial LLM lifecycle: vendors sunset models on fixed dates to cut serving costs and push customers onto better infrastructure. For teams that hard-coded GPT-4o prompts, tool schemas, and output parsers into production, a dated sunset turns an abstract upgrade into a mandatory engineering project with a deadline.
key_points: OpenAI has published a migration guide with a firm January 2027 cutoff for GPT-4o and related GPT-4.x models. The recommended path is evaluating GPT-6 Luna on representative workloads first, then rolling out gradually. The playbook is four steps: establish a quality, latency, and cost baseline; evaluate Luna; tune prompts and settings; then shift production traffic in stages while monitoring.

The default recommended setting is reasoning effort set to 'none', which OpenAI expects will cover most existing GPT-4.x use cases. Teams can raise the setting if they need more quality, accepting extra latency and cost. This matters because reasoning settings can change token consumption dramatically, so a 'cheaper' model is not automatically a cheaper bill.

GPT-6 Luna carries a lower per-token price than the GPT-4.x models it replaces, and OpenAI frames it as more capable at that lower price. But the guide explicitly warns that total cost depends on token usage and reasoning configuration, so teams should compare end-to-end task cost on their own traffic rather than trusting list prices.

Migration is behavioral, not just a model-string swap. OpenAI tells developers to verify output formatting, tool and function calling, and other behaviors their applications depend on, then adjust prompts and verbosity before retesting. Edge cases are called out specifically, since those are where silent regressions tend to surface after cutover.

Support is split by account type: self-serve customers reach OpenAI through the help chat bubble, while sales-managed customers can request an engineering-backed migration plan tailored to their product. That tiering signals OpenAI treats large enterprise migrations as a retention problem worth staffed engineering time.
report.impact: For the industry, this reinforces a faster, more vendor-controlled release cadence, where model retirement dates become procurement deadlines and pricing pressure from open-weight rivals keeps flowing through. For developers, the real cost is engineering time: re-running evals, rewriting prompt scaffolding, re-validating tool calls and output schemas, and monitoring for regressions during a staged rollout. The upside is a genuine chance to cut inference spend and simplify to one model family. For regular users, the change is mostly invisible until it isn't: assistants and third-party apps built on GPT-4o may subtly shift tone, formatting, or behavior after an unannounced backend swap, and any tool that let users pin GPT-4o will lose that option.
report.tools: To run this migration safely, pair OpenAI's GPT-6 developer guide with an evaluation harness: OpenAI Evals or promptfoo for regression suites, LangSmith, Braintrust, or W&B Weave for tracing and scoring, LiteLLM or OpenRouter for routing and A/B shadow traffic, and Helicone or Langfuse for per-request cost and latency monitoring before you flip the switch.
